::: {.project-lede}
Repeated observations and independent dyads contribute different kinds of information. This program studies how target estimands, multilevel structure, role parameterization, random effects, and design features determine what longitudinal dyadic data can support when the number of dyads is limited.
:::

## Accepted Paper {#accepted-paper}

**Liu, L.** (accepted). *Longitudinal dyadic modeling with limited numbers of dyads: Aligning estimands, information sources, and multilevel structure*. **Methods in Psychology**.

The paper develops an **estimand-information alignment** framework: each target dyadic estimand should be evaluated in relation to the level of the design that supplies its statistical information. The study distinguishes fixed-effect precision, repeated-sampling calibration, model completion, optimizer convergence, and support for random-effect structure rather than treating them as a single notion of model performance.

## Research Design {#design}

The accepted study combines three complementary components.

::: {.design-grid}
::: {.design-box}
<div class="design-label">Benchmark</div>
<div class="design-value">100 dyads × 21 occasions</div>
:::

::: {.design-box}
<div class="design-label">Subsampling</div>
<div class="design-value">10 · 20 · 30 · 50 dyads</div>
:::

::: {.design-box}
<div class="design-label">Monte Carlo</div>
<div class="design-value">56 conditions</div>
:::

::: {.design-box}
<div class="design-label">Replications</div>
<div class="design-value">1,000 / condition</div>
:::
:::

The Monte Carlo design varies dyad count, repeated-measure intensity, dyad-level variance, residual dependence, and between-person predictor dispersion. Across the simulation, **56,000 model fits** were requested. Performance was evaluated using bias, RMSE, confidence-interval coverage, standard-error calibration, Type I error, singularity, variance-component behavior, and fixed-effect precision.

## Key Findings {#key-findings}

::: {.mini-grid}
<div><strong>Random effects</strong><br><span>Limited dyad replication most clearly reduced support for dyad-level random-effect structure.</span></div>
<div><strong>Fixed effects</strong><br><span>Bias remained small and confidence-interval coverage was close to nominal across the examined conditions.</span></div>
<div><strong>Within-person precision</strong><br><span>Increasing occasions from 7 to 21 reduced interval widths by about 42%.</span></div>
<div><strong>Between-person precision</strong><br><span>The same increase in occasions reduced interval widths by only about 6%.</span></div>
:::

The practical implication is that **more repeated measurements cannot be treated as a substitute for more independent dyads**. Repeated occasions add substantial information for within-person estimands, while between-dyad parameters and higher-level random effects depend more strongly on independent dyad replication.

## Code {#code}

The accepted article includes a public simulated pedagogical benchmark and supplementary analysis materials. I will link the final public data/code location here once the journal version and repository are released.

## Contribution to my research program

This program extends my broader work on **multilevel inference under limited higher-level information** into longitudinal interpersonal data. It links design, estimands, random-effect support, and practical modeling decisions rather than treating sample size as a single undifferentiated quantity.
